analysis.one_liner: Bans the president, members of Congress, Supreme Court justices, and Fed officials from trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and top Federal Reserve officials from holding or trading individual stocks, futures, commodities, and certain cryptocurrencies, and would require them to sell any such holdings within 120 days. It would also require senior officials to disclose any federal loans, contracts, or grants they or their families receive, replace the criminal penalty for late trade reports with a fixed fine, and require financial disclosures to be posted online in searchable, downloadable formats. The bill never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want to know whether the people writing laws and setting monetary policy hold financial stakes in the companies those decisions affect. The bill would remove officials' ability to profit from trading on nonpublic information about legislation, regulation, or Federal Reserve actions, and would make officials' financial disclosures far easier for the public to search online.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered officials from holding, buying, or selling individual securities, futures, commodities, and certain cryptocurrencies, and from holding net short positions, with violations fined at least 10 percent of the value of the interest [S2].

Requires members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and Federal Reserve bank officials to divest covered holdings within 120 days, with limited extensions made public [S2].

Requires covered officials and their spouses and dependent children to report applications for and receipt of federal loans, contracts, and grants within set deadlines, with a $5,000 fine for failures to report [S2].

Requires financial disclosure and stock transaction reports for members of Congress, senior executive branch officials, judicial officers, and Federal Reserve bank officials to be filed electronically and published online in searchable, sortable, downloadable formats with an API [S2].
Extends existing financial disclosure and anti-insider-trading requirements under title 5 and the STOCK Act to presidents, vice presidents, and directors of Federal Reserve banks [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and senior Federal Reserve officials who currently hold or trade individual stocks, futures, commodities, or covered crypto assets would have to divest them within 120 days and could only keep diversified mutual funds and Treasury securities. Officials whose spouses earn stock compensation at an operating business are exempted for that compensation [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress, justices, Fed and administration officials

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces the current criminal penalty for failing to file a stock transaction report with a fixed $1,000 fine per failure, which critics could argue weakens the existing penalty even as it adds a broader trading ban [S2].

Enforcement depends on the same supervising ethics offices that administer current disclosure rules; the bill sets fine amounts but relies on those offices to issue regulations and pursue violations, and a $5,000 or $1,000 fixed fine may be small relative to the value of the trades involved [S2].

The ban covers officials' spouses and dependent children but exempts a spouse's compensation and stock from their primary employer, which leaves a channel through which a household can still hold significant single-company stock [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: officials would lose the ability to hold or trade individual stocks and would face forced divestiture, in exchange for a public that can more easily see and trust officials' finances. The design has defensible weaknesses — fixed fines replace potential criminal penalties for late trade reports, and a spouse's employer stock remains exempt — but the trading ban, divestiture clock, and searchable online disclosures are concrete, enforceable-on-paper rules aimed directly at conflicts of interest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Katie Porter introduced the bill on December 15, 2023, near the end of the first session of the 118th Congress [S1].
It was referred to the Oversight and Accountability, House Administration, and Judiciary committees [S4].
The bill had one cosponsor, a Democrat, and no further committee or floor action appears in its action history through the end of the Congress [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, Supreme Court justices, and senior executive and Federal Reserve officials, who keep their current ability to hold and trade individual stocks and whose disclosures remain harder for the public to search.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent officeholders who keep trading rights

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and senior federal officials
industries.note: The bill would force them to divest individual stocks, futures, commodities, and covered crypto and fine violations at 10 percent of the value involved. Their interest in keeping the current rules runs against the public's interest in knowing whether decision-makers hold stakes in the outcomes they control.

Fed bank presidents, vice presidents, and directors would be brought under financial disclosure and insider-trading rules for the first time and banned from covered trading. The bill would also require their disclosures to be posted in searchable public databases.

Justices would be covered by the trading ban and divestiture requirement and their disclosures would move to searchable electronic filing. Currently judicial disclosure is handled separately from the congressional system.
